module.title: Checking and reporting
module.summary: How to verify a suspicious request safely and report it so colleagues are protected.

blocks.title: Checking and reporting
blocks.body: Noticing a warning sign is only half the job. Here you will practise checking a request safely and reporting it the right way.
blocks.accessibility: All content is available as text.

blocks.title: Verify through a separate channel
blocks.body:
If a message asks for something unusual, check it **outside the message**: call the sender on a number you already know, or type the organisation’s address into your browser yourself.

Do not use the phone number, link or reply address in the suspicious email — they may lead straight back to the attacker.
blocks.accessibility: All content is available as text.

blocks.title: From suspicion to report
blocks.body: Follow the same short sequence every time a message makes you pause.
blocks.accessibility: All content is available as text.

blocks.title: Why reporting quickly matters
blocks.body: Early reports let the security team warn colleagues and block the campaign before more people interact with it. If you have **already clicked** or entered details, report straight away — speed matters more than embarrassment.
blocks.accessibility: All content is available as text.

blocks.title: Choose the safe check
blocks.accessibility: All content is available as text.

interaction.stem: A supplier emails new bank details for this month’s invoice. What is the safest way to check?

options.text: Reply to the email and ask them to confirm
Call the supplier on the number already held in your records
Call the number in the email signature

interaction.feedbackCorrect: Yes — a contact route you already trust cannot be controlled by the sender of the suspicious email.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Contact details inside a suspicious email may belong to the attacker. Use a route you already hold.

optionFeedback.text: A reply goes back to whoever sent the message.
The signature is part of the suspicious message.

interaction.rationale: Independent verification uses a channel the attacker does not control.

blocks.title: Order the steps
blocks.accessibility: All content is available as text.

interaction.stem: Put the response steps in order.

options.text: Pause — do not click or reply

interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Start by pausing, verify separately, then report.
interaction.rationale: Pausing prevents harm; verifying and reporting protect you and colleagues.

items.label: Pause
items.detail: Do not click, open or reply

items.label: Report

textEquivalent.short: Five-step process from pausing to reporting a suspicious email
textEquivalent.long: Step 1, pause: do not click, open attachments or reply. Step 2, check the warning signs: sender, links, request and tone. Step 3, verify through a separate known contact route. Step 4, report using the report button or security mailbox. Step 5, delete the message after reporting.

visuals.title: Why speed matters: illustrative reporting timeline
visuals.purpose: Illustrate that earlier reports protect more colleagues (illustrative figures, not statistics).

textEquivalent.short: Illustrative bar chart: later reports mean more colleagues exposed
textEquivalent.long: An illustrative bar chart, not real data: if the first report arrives within 5 minutes, about 2 colleagues have opened the email; within 1 hour, about 9; if reported the next day, about 24. Earlier reporting limits exposure.
